scenes.actionText:
A beautiful home somewhere in the California country. A bluebird sky and gentle breeze coming through the window and... a WIDE OPEN BACK DOOR. Eerie music.
The camera begins a slow crawl, until we discover why we’re at floor level: A BROKEN BOTTLE OF WHISKEY, shattered across the floor. The camera stays focused here as:
A pair of BOOTS enters the frame, hastily running to check that open door (but not closing it). We stay at GROUND LEVEL, so we don’t see a face. There’s panic in his movements, though. It’s the feeling of having interrupted something awful. Eerie music swells...
The BOOTS run back to a CLOSET, kneeling down to open A SAFE. A SECOND FIGURE EMERGES FROM BEHIND A DOOR. All we see is shoes and jeans and nothing else. The second figure quickly, deftly, calmly, steps through that open back door and escapes, but not without:
The CREAK of a floorboard. Our man comes running, only to find NOTHING and NO ONE THERE. Eerie music climaxing until...

scenes.actionText:
CLOSE ON: Sawyer (33), attractive but also quiet, cerebral, nervous. Dressed to blend with the background. She shifts in her chair. We can hear people clearing throats and stirring off camera. Sunshine beams through a window behind her.

Sawyer:
  What am I trying to say? Like he was quick-witted, but he knew almost nothing. About anything. I’d explain things to him, and he’d get this slack-jawed look, like.
She does the face: mouth agape, a bewildered frown.

Sawyer:
  But he also had this wit. He had this canon of in-jokes that he’d spin and reference and callback--like Tubby Time.
Off the looks she’s getting:

Sawyer:
  He’d joke about taking baths with his brother, Aaron, and he called it “Tubby time.” That was the whole joke, that he and Aaron would soap each other’s backs and clean each other’s ears and it just got grosser and weirder--
  ((laughing to herself))
  He was ridiculous. All the time. Every hour of the day. Even when it felt like the world was the most fucked, he had a joke about it. Maybe especially when it felt the most fucked. When I imagined the person I’d end up with--he checked none of the boxes. I got blind-sided by this imperfect, unexpected guy who just made me feel calm and happy and loved. When we first met it was under...
  ((beat))
  Difficult circumstances. I thought he was a jackass. And when I felt it happening, I pretty much begged myself not to let it happen. I was stunned at myself. What I was capable of--
  ((clears her throat))
  But we ended up together for five years, married for four, and I could never get enough of him. He’d leave me two-minute long voice notes with his thoughts on Iron Maiden. He came home from a bar drunk one time and for forty minutes just ranked his favorite episodes of “Caroline in the City” while he stood in the kitchen and ate an entire loaf of Hawaiian bread. Once, at a party around some of my colleagues, he pretended like he didn’t know what a PhD was. Like he thought it was a drug, like PCP, and he told them he married me because he needed to get his hands on some “PhD.” Then he started snorting the dinner table and rubbing his gums. And I was like-- “Okay, this is love.”
A beat as she wipes her tears.

Sawyer:
  When he died, we had him embalmed, and the process accidentally gave his corpse this enormous erection. Obviously, we couldn’t have that at an open casket, so the mortician asked me what to do with it, and the only thing I could think was, ya know, cut it off. But I knew he’d be miserable not having his penis buried with him, so I told them to put it up his ass. Then at the funeral, I leaned down and whispered to him, “I told you it fucking hurts.”
PULL BACK TO REVEAL: She’s not sitting in any kind of group therapy session. This is a HOTEL CONFERENCE ROOM littered with POP-UP BANNERS: DAYANET ANALYTICS ANNUAL WELLNESS & EMPOWERMENT WEEK.
All the participants, including Sawyer sit on bean bags and stability balls.
She looks around as her joke falls flat on the others, including her boss, SCOTT (40s, bland).

SAWYER:
  See, that’s the kind of joke he would’ve loved.

Scott:
  Okay, Sawyer, thank you. I think we’re good on “two truths and a lie.” Maybe the egg drop meditation next?
TITLE CARD: BACK IN YOUR ARMS

scenes.actionText:
Sawyer eats dinner with JUSTINE and TOM (60s), her dead husband’s parents, as well as her brother-in-law, AARON (30s) and his wife, NADIA (30s).

JustINE:
  You told that joke??

Aaron:
  Forget the joke--you told them about Tubby Time?!

Sawyer:
  Fucking blend of wellness fluff and tech culture. It’s so anesthetizing I end up vomiting up my life story.

aaron:
  Tubby Time is a sacred family tradition, Sawyer.

Sawyer:
  So I’ve heard.

aARON:
  We soaped each other’s backs.

tom:
  Wait, what is Tubby Time?
  This dumb joke these two had--

AARON:
  A sacred family tradition that kept our ears and nips squeaky clean, babe!

tom:
  I still do not get Millennials.

justine:
  ((to Sawyer))
  Soy, hon, you clearly need to talk about this stuff. I’d love it if you tried going back to group therapy.

SawYER:
  I know you’d love it, Justine. The relevant question is how I feel about it. You don’t understand just how many banal stories there are of loved ones leaving behind a “sign.” All the songs on the radio can’t be from your dead husband, Marcia.
Aaron cracks up. Justine is exasperated.

SaWYER:
  I hate performing that way.

Aaron:
  Maybe just knowing the time and place for a dead husband joke.

SAWYER:
  ((to Aaron))
  How can you tell your husband’s dead?

Aaron:
  How?

SAWYER:
  The sex gets better.
Aaron and Sawyer slap a well-practiced pro-basketball-player style high five. Nadia looks like she’s bored with the routine.

Justine:
  No one is asking you to perform. But if you don’t talk about it, your grief will fester in unhealthy ways--

Nadia:
  Is there any way we could switch topics?

Justine:
  Sure! What do you want to talk about, Nadia? Politics? Dating as a widow? Avoidant attachment styles?

Tom:
  Why don’t you three get together for a thruple?

Nadia:
  Eww. Tom--

Sawyer:
  Tom, c’mon--

Tom:
  Sorry, sorry, I was trying out some millennial humor!

Aaron:
  I haven’t had a threesome since I dated men in my twenties.

Nadia:
  What about Oscar?

Aaron:
  Since I dated men in my thirties.

Justine:
  Oh, how sweet!

Sipping a glass of wine, Sawyer gently zooms in on the picture she took of KENDRICK that morning. She’s transfixed, almost as if instead of using her fingers to zoom, she can change the shape of his face to precisely match David’s.
KNOCK-KNOCK!
SAWYER JUMPS. She looks to the door. Hesitates. She goes to the door and checks the keyhole. She answers.
MARGO (50s) an earthy, friendly woman with a preponderance of bracelets and funky earrings holds a BOTTLE OF WINE. She looks at Sawyer’s glass.

Margo:
  Oh! You were thinking what I was thinking.

SAWYER:
  Excuse me?

  ((holding out the wine))
  For you! I’m Margo. I’m your neighbor down the road.

SAWYER:
  Down the road--

MARGO:
  I saw you moving in and thought, Ah that looks like a chance to stack up some karma and dharma and all that.
She hands over the wine.

SAWYER:
  Thank you. I’m Sawyer.

MARGO:
  New to town?

SAWYER:
  That’s right.

MARGO:
  Well, just wanted to say hi, and I’m around if you need any tips, advice, borrow some sugar--whatever. This town can be a bit of shock to the system. Pace of life is slower here.

SAWYER:
  How long have you lived here?

MARGO:
  Never left! Anyway, don’t want to bother you, but I’m around if you need me.
She turns to leave and Sawyer makes a decision.

SAWYER:
  Actually. I don’t know a single person here. If you wanted to grab dinner sometime? I don’t cook--

MARGO:
  What is this the Fifties? Neither do I. But I know the best takeout spots in town.

SAWYER:
  I’d love that.

MARGO:
  Here’s my number.
She holds her phone up to Sawyer’s to transfer the info.

MARGO:
  Welcome to Solvang, kid.
Sawyer shuts the door, happy. She’s made a friend.
She picks up her wine and walks over to: a CORKBOARD fixed to the living room wall. She’s pinned to it a MAP OF SOLVANG. She stares. She sips.
She looks at a box of RED PUSH-PINS. Shaking her head at herself, how insane this is. Nevertheless...
Right where Jason Kendrick’s house is, she pushes in a RED PUSHPIN.
She assesses her work as the get-shit-done beat returns.
She tilts her head like: OK. You’re really doing this.

Sawyer sits waiting in the dim quiet, deep in thought. So much so that when Kendrick approaches her...

JaSON KENDRICK:
  Hey.

SaWYER:
  Oh! Hi! Sorry. I was wool-gathering.

JASON KENDRICK:
  My bad...

SAWYER:
  ((stumbling))
  I zone out sometimes. My mom used to say I live in my own reality.
  ((pointing outside))
  Is that your car?

JASON KENDRICK:
  ((taking a seat))
  The Defender? Yeah, I know. Every time I turn it on, a polar bear dies.

SAWYER:
  No, it’s great. Very... big--is it diesel?

JASON KENDRICK:
  Yeah, that’s right. You know cars?

SAWYER:
  I’m just wondering how you got it certified in California?

JASON KENDRICK:
  Okay, I lied. You actually have to feed the engine a baby penguin to start it.
They exchange a smile as he cracks the menu.
LATER: They face each other. Drinks between them.

JASON KENDRICK:
  So where were you before this?

SAWYER:
  Minneapolis.

JASON KENDRICK:
  That’s a big change.

SAWYER:
  I needed warm weather.

JASON KENDRICK:
  What kind of work do you do?

SAWYER:
  Well, before this I taught English. Seventh graders.
Kendrick looks up at her, suddenly much more intrigued.

JASON KENDRICK:
  No shit? My mom taught English. Same grade.

SAWYER:
  Oh really? Wow. So she probably had the whole curriculum. Freak the Mighty, On the Far Side of the Mountain--

JASON KENDRICK:
  Where the Red Fern Grows, The Outsiders--
  Hatchet.

JASON KENDRICK:
  Hatchet.

JASON KENDRICK:
  ((cracking up))
  Oh my God! Hatchet! My favorite fucking book at age twelve.

SAWYER:
  He’s a boy surviving in the wilderness with nothing but a hatchet. What’s not to love?

JASON KENDRICK:
  He cuts trees with the hatchet, he starts a fire with the hatchet...

SAWYER:
  A simple premise that translates to a universal quest for survival.

JASON KENDRICK:
  But you’re not teaching anymore?

SAWYER:
  I’d been wanting to move on. But it took a bad divorce and his alimony payments before I could afford to.

JASON KENDRICK:
  Oh. I’m sorry to hear that.
  ((holds up his drink))
  Welcome to the club.
They clink.

JASON KENDRICK:
  Divorced two years now, but the marriage went to shit well before that. It’s not so bad. You learn to hate them and yourself a little less with each passing day.

SaWYER:
  And what is it that you do in Solvang?

JASON KENDRICK:
  I’m an actor actually. But not in Solvang. A real actor.

SAWYER:
  Sorry. I don’t watch many movies.

JASON KENDRICK:
  TV mostly. I was on this show...
  ((trails off))
  Never mind.

SAWYER:
  No! That’s so great. What kind of show? What was it called? Sorry, I feel stupid right now.

JASON KENDRICK:
  I’m the one who feels stupid, trust me. I made my name on a show called XenoSouls.

SAWYER:
  XenoSouls?

JASON KENDRICK:
  ((smirking))
  That’s right. It was about this detective who stumbles onto a conspiracy, a race of aliens living amongst us, disguised as regular people.

SAWYER:
  Oh, that sounds...

JASON KENDRICK:
  Cheesy as fuck. Derivative as all hell. I know. But, ya know, every once in a while the writing could be zippy. A little fun. It was kind of incredible for a while there.

SAWYER:
  But it’s not anymore?

JASON KENDRICK:
  I’m trying not to lead with any woe-is-me actor stories. There is nothing worse than an actor complaining about his lot in life.

SAWYER:
  Try me.
She is attentive, eyes wide, ready. She plays with her hair.

JASON KENDRICK:
  The show ended. Right? As shows do. So I tried to make a few movies. And it was just a rude awakening, like, Oh, not everything will be successful. Oh, maybe I have bad taste in scripts. Oh, maybe the prior thing was a fluke.
  ((a beat))
  I never had any dreams of being Tom Cruise or Daniel Day Lewis or, hell, even Freddie Prinze Jr.--

SAWYER:
  Now you’ve really lost me.

JASON KENDRICK:
  ((laughing))
  All I ever wanted was something sustainable, so I wouldn’t have to be slinging Nissans back in Jersey. But then I got this big role, and it was the most money I’d ever seen in my life and...

SAWYER:
  And what?

JASON KENDRICK:
  Nah. Nothing. I’m talking too much. How was your divorce?

SAWYER:
  My divorce?

JASON KENDRICK:
  Yeah. If it was enough to send you fleeing, must’ve been a good one.

SAWYER:
  I don’t know--what happens in any marriage that sours?

JASON KENDRICK:
  He cheats.

SAWYER:
  No. Never.
  ((beat))
  We just. It just. It became something else. Why? Did you cheat?

JASON KENDRICK:
  No. When we got married, my wife and I said we’d have a Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell policy. You know, when it came to extracurriculars. We both worked in the game, in the world of celebrity, and with that comes a certain amount of temptation you can never really be rid of. For a while it worked. Then it didn’t.

SAWYER:
  What happened? You fell in love? She fell in love?

JASON KENDRICK:
  You got a way of asking questions without answering any.

SAWYER:
  I’m sorry. I’m just interested.
Kendrick assesses her. She’s playing with her hair again.

JASON KENDRICK:
  Not sure I’m ready to spill my entire divorce on a first date.

SAWYER:
  Fair enough. Maybe on Date Two we can wander around a mall or something like we’re fourteen...

JASON KENDRICK:
  A mall?
  ((scoffs))
  Don’t think I’ve been to a mall in twenty years.

JaSON KENDRICK:
  Back to my original question...

SAWYER:
  Which was...?

JASON KENDRICK:
  Why a middle school teacher wanted to drop everything and move out here.

SAWYER:
  Isn’t California where everyone goes for a second chance?

JASON KENDRICK:
  Not with our housing prices.

SAWYER:
  Sometimes, when your life has been completely turned upside-down, when you had all these goals to have kids, a family, a life with a person, and it all falls apart...
  ((beat))
  I needed a drastic change. And even if it didn’t exactly make sense, here I am sitting with you. And I like the way your forehead pinches when you’re thinking.

I tried to make an indie movie with this ego-crazed director, thinks he’s fucking PTA, and I had to bail halfway through, we hated each other so much. So instead I made a big CGI trash pile that lost some $70 million. Then right after that...
  ((beat))

So as soon as we could, we headed up there to sift around in the rubble and look for VINs on the burnt-out frames. Lilly wanted to hire someone to do it, but I just needed to see. So there we were in N95s, sifting around in the ashes. I just couldn’t believe my eyes. Here, I thought I’d been living fearlessly, living for the moment, seize the day, all that shit. But looking at my home and everything I’d ever owned and everything I’d ever accomplished in all those years in Los Angeles suddenly vaporized. That’s when I knew Lilly was going to leave me. I kinda fell apart. I couldn’t work, I couldn’t focus, I was acting erratic.

scenes.actionText:
Sawyer enters. She’s anxious, edgy, maybe near a breakdown of some kind. She sets the bottle on the counter.

SaWYER:
  I just wanted to--I told you I’m not good at this. I’m not good at dating. I just wanted to ask if I did anything wrong at dinner the other night. I don’t know, I feel like maybe I made a fool of myself with all that Vaudeville stuff...
They stand in the middle of the kitchen. All the dishes are still dirty from the night before.
The KITCHEN KNIFE still lies on the cutting board, in the frame but not central. Just visible.

JASON KENDRICK:
  A fool?

SAWYER:
  Yeah. If I said something. Or did something.
He points at her with his whiskey-glass hand.

JASON KENDRICK:
  How did you know I’m from Pennsauken?

SAWYER:
  Huh?
  ((beat))
  You told me that.

JASON KENDRICK:
  Right. I think I told you I was from Jersey.

SAWYER:
  Well. I did a quick Google. And Wikipedia.

JASON KENDRICK:
  Okay, Pennsauken ain’t on my Wikipedia page. It’s wrong on there and says Palmyra--but whatever. When we met, though, you just guessed I was an Eagles fan?

SAWYER:
  Jason, it’s really not a big deal. All I did was look you up--

JASON KENDRICK:
  How did you know about the bathroom?

Sawyer:
  What about it?

Jason Kendrick:
  When you were over for dinner, you knew the bathroom light was on the outside of the door.
Sawyer’s eyes land on the bedroom behind him. She sees the SAFE is open.

JASON KENDRICK:
  Who are you?
  ((off Sawyer’s confusion))
  Who are you?

SAWYER:
  I don’t understand.

JASON KENDRICK:
  Let’s try this: what school did you teach at?

SAWYER:
  In Minneapolis.

JASON KENDRICK:
  That’s a city. I said, “What school?”
Sawyer stares at him. He holds up his phone with the picture of her driver’s license.

JASON KENDRICK:
  It’s not just celebrities you can Google, Sawyer. You’re an economist? You have a PhD. You did your dissertation on
  ((reads from phone))
  “Social Drivers of Digital Transformation Economics for IT, AI, and Machine Learning.”
Sawyer just stands there.

JASON KENDRICK:
  And you knew where my bathroom light was. That light confuses everyone. You didn’t ask. You didn’t hesitate. You went straight to it.
Sawyer says nothing.

JASON KENDRICK:
  It was you in my house, wasn’t it? Everyone thought I was losing my fucking mind, but I knew someone had been in here. I knew it.

SAWYER:
  Jason, I--
Tucked into his pants, he pulls from behind him: THE GUN. It dangles from his arm, pointing at the ground.

JASON KENDRICK:
  I want you to leave. Now.
Sawyer stares at the gun, breathless. But she doesn’t move.

JASON KENDRICK:
  ((furious))
  Get out of my house, you crazy fucking cunt!
A beat. Sawyer stares. The knife is within arm’s reach. Her eyes don’t go there at all. But ours do.

SaWYER:
  You look like him. Just like him.

JASON KENDRICK:
  ((beat))
  What? What are you talking about?

SAWYER:
  My husband. I’m not divorced. He died. A pulmonary embolism. Out of nowhere. No warning. I just came downstairs one night--we were about to watch a show--and there he was lying on the floor, not breathing.
Kendrick still looks furious but he doesn’t interrupt her.

SAWYER:
  His name was David. We’d bought a house. We were trying to get pregnant. He and I--we had to fight to be together. I had to give up everything. He and I used to joke, that he looked like you. Or you looked like him. We loved your show, and you became a little in-joke we had. He’d do your voice, recite lines. It isn’t just the physical resemblance either. It’s little tics. Small mannerisms. You’re... brasher than he was. He was gentler, good-humored, and not sad in the same way you’re sad.
On Kendrick, this lands. She’s seen into him somehow.

SAWYER:
  Coming here, to find you--I just wanted a sliver of that back. Even if it’s fake. I wanted to make love to you. Just once. I know that sounds insane, I know I sound insane, and I swear I’m not some crazy stalker, I’m just--
  ((beat, crying now))
  I just want to touch your chest and arms like I did with him him. I want to make love to you like you’re him. I want to put your cock in my mouth like I did with him. And I want to fall asleep beside you. Like you’re him.
On Kendrick staring at her in stunned silence. Absolutely still. The gun dangling from his hand.

Anna opens the car door as Sawyer emerges.

Anna:

  ((beat))

anna:

She starts to get inside the car.

ANNA:

SAWYER:
  This will never be over?

ANNA:
  This?
She shakes her head in amazement. Slams the car door shut.

AnNA:
  You mean “this” when you fucked my fiancé. When you stole him and married him and ruined my life? Is that the “this” you’re referring to, Sawyer?

SAWYER:
  He’s gone, Anna. David’s gone.

ANNA:
  Oh, I know. But you at least got those years with him. My grief just got a fresh new twist. The man I planned a life with, who left me for my fucking sister, died. And all I can think, after all these years, is how much I still hate him... and how much I miss him.
  ((crying, shakes her head))
  The thing is I saw it happening. I saw the way you two acted around each other. I just told myself it couldn’t actually be real. I was imagining jealousies the way I’d always imagined them with you since we were teenagers.

SAWYER:
  I told you, nothing ever happened while you guys were together--

ANNA:
  That’s not the point! Do you understand at all, Sawyer? It’s been five years, and I’m stuck. Completely stuck. I had to take a job in Germany just to get away from you! And I can’t date, I can’t move on, I still can’t think about anything else. And I can’t be around my sister because you just remind me of--
She breaks down, unable to continue.

SAWYER:
  I’m sorry, Anna. I’m so sorry. I’ve always been sorry.

ANNA:
  Before Mom died, she warned me, too. She knew something about being fucked over by a man. She told me there was something happening between you and David, and I told her it was impossible. “Sawyer would never do that.”

SAWYER:
  We were in love, Anna. I don’t have any defense besides that.

ANNA:
  What is that worth?

SAWYER:
  I need you. I’ve needed you so badly. I miss both of you so much I feel like I’m drowning.

ANNA:
  And that’s why I can’t forgive you. There has to be a consequence for what you did. And even if it kills me, Sawyer--even if shutting you out costs me my sanity--I swear to fucking God, I will make you live with the consequence. I will never forgive you, and this will never be right.

SAWYER:
  I’m not asking you to forgive me--

ANNA:
  What the fuck are you asking then?!

SAWYER:
  Just... wait here. One minute.
Sawyer turns and goes as fast as she can back inside the house.
Frustrated, Anna grinds her heel into the gravel and waits.
Sawyer returns, holding: the MACARONI CROWN. She hands it to Anna.

SAWYER:
  I’ve been meaning to... When I cleaned out the house, I found it. But it’s yours. I was more your court jester than anything.
Anna doesn’t give it another glance. She just stares at Sawyer like: This fucking bitch still doesn’t get it.
She drops the Crown in the dirt. She turns, gets back in her rental car, and drives away.

Jason sits on the couch as Sawyer hands him a cup of coffee.

JASON KENDRICK:

  ((reassuring))

Kendrick shakes his head.

JASON KENDRICK:
  I knew she was dangerous. It was like the more I tried to tell everyone, the more they thought I was overreacting.

SAWYER:
  She must’ve started following me after I started following you. She told me her name was Margo. And that she was a local Reiki healer.

JASON KENDRICK:
  She is. Just in LA. We--
  ((he rephrases))
  I was drunk at this party, and I thought she knew it would be a one-time--it doesn’t matter.
  ((beat))
  I’m sorry about your husband.

SAWYER:
  Thank you.

JASON KENDRICK:
  I think that’s why I was attracted to you when we first met. I could sense you had something similar.

SAWYER:
  Similar how?

JASON KENDRICK:
  I dunno what to call it. A knowledge.
  ((his voice gets shaky))
  After I slept with her, that woman started texting me all the time, leaving voicemails, commenting on every post I’d ever put up on social media. I had to change my number. Then she started showing up--at the grocery store or near the set of the show. Never crossing the line enough to where I could do anything about it.
  ((beat))
  But when the fires started, I was sure it was her, that the bitch had finally snapped. And she wasn’t just going to take my house, she was going to burn down the whole city. Later, even after it was all said and done, I still had a hard time believing it was just the Santa Ana winds.
  ((beat))
  When we got the alert, Lilly and I ran outside, to get in one of our three cars to get the fuck outta there, and over the hill, I could see this awful orange glow. For a full ten seconds I couldn’t move. I couldn’t even reach for the door handle. I was just totally paralyzed.
  ((beat))
  Afterwards, I couldn’t get rid of this... terror. It’s like I’m still standing frozen by the car waiting for the fire to come over the hill. And there’s nothing I can do but buy bullshit online and try not to think about it all too much. When I bought that gun, I told myself it was for protection. From her. But obviously that's not what it was for. It was in case I couldn't be alone with my thoughts any longer.
A long beat passes between them.

JASON KENDRICK:
  ((half-joking))
  So. You wanna get a drink sometime?

SAWYER:
  If you’re ever in Minneapolis, you can look me up.
Kendrick lets a wan smile slip at this soft, careful rejection.

SAWYER:

She holds out his sweaty, crumpled running shirt.
